# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
> — Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial* (1969) [@Simon1969SciencesArtificial]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Herbert Simon defined design through the course from a
present situation to a preferred one. The definition places problem choice,
abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs inside the technical work.
Automation can contribute substantially to that course. The architect's
technical contribution lies in shaping the course into a coherent system and
deciding which design should advance.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
If a capable AI-assisted design system can formulate studies, generate
artifacts, search design spaces, run tools, interpret failures, and recommend
a design, what technical work do architects still contribute?
:::

Grant the strongest premise in this book. A capable AI-assisted system can
perform substantial work from study formulation through technical
recommendation, including coordinating specialized methods, tools,
verification, and failure-driven revision across a long design study. Nothing
in this chapter depends on preserving a protected set of tasks that only people
can perform.

The architect's role is not whatever automation has failed to absorb. It is a
positive technical role. Architects frame the problem, choose the abstractions
and system boundaries, compose components and disciplines into one feasible
design, interpret disagreement and missing evidence, and decide which
uncertainties a product can carry. They design both the system and the process
that designs alongside them.

The distinctive output of this work is an architecture commitment. It names
the design that may advance, the conditions and evidence that support that
choice, the remaining risk, and the evidence that must narrow or reopen it.
The commitment is useful only while those conditions remain true.

Here, *the architect* means the authorized technical role that carries this
system view. One lead architect may hold it, or a team may divide it among
specialists. In either case, the scope of each decision, required concurrence,
escalation path, and responsibility for end-to-end integration must remain
explicit.

Organizational assignments vary. Here, *commitment authority* means the named
role or set of roles assigned to decide whether a design advances. When
architecture and product authority reside in separate roles, both must concur.

This role exists even when every component works as intended. A model can
optimize a network link against the objective it was given, a compiler can
validate a lowering path, a verifier can return a counterexample, and a
physical-design flow can close timing. The architecture problem remains
whether these results describe one product under one consistent set of
workload, software, interface, memory, power, package, and product
assumptions.

The chapter therefore moves from capability to commitment. It first separates
the architecture result, the assessment of the AI-assisted program, and the
decision to advance a particular architecture. It then develops the
architect's technical work in problem framing, abstraction, component choice,
cross-layer integration, and interpretation. Only after that work is visible
does it address bounded commitment and the responsibility that continues when
conditions change.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Separate an architecture result, an AI program assessment, and an
  architecture commitment.
- Frame an architecture problem whose workload, software path, system
  boundary, constraints, and decision remain coherent as AI and tools act.
- Choose abstractions, methods, components, interfaces, and checks that fit
  the technical problem rather than merely the available automation.
- Integrate specialist results across software, ISA, microarchitecture,
  memory, implementation, package, power, and product concerns.
- Interpret disagreement and uncertainty, make a bounded design commitment,
  and state what later evidence must reopen it.
:::

## Architectural Practice with Capable Assistance

A weak account of the architect's role begins with a list of tasks that current
models cannot perform. That account expires as capability improves. A stronger
account asks which technical decisions give a capable design system
architectural meaning.

Delegability depends on the conditions around the work, not on reserving a task
for people. A bounded array-mapping sweep or tool run can be assigned to a
method or specialist when the candidate state is observable, changes are
reversible, independent checks can reject a bad result, and cross-layer
consequences are bounded. Freezing a software-facing interface is different.
It is a difficult-to-reverse cross-layer decision that hardens assumptions
across compiler and runtime behavior, memory, RTL, physical implementation,
and product integration. A qualified architecture role must reconcile that
evidence, and the commitment authority must decide whether the transition
proceeds. Both cases also depend on a team competent to challenge assumptions
and trace a failure beyond the delegated boundary.

This is a technical assignment rule, not a task reservation or a claim about
which jobs automation can absorb. Architecture practice still turns on six
connected judgments. Architects formulate the system question, choose
representations and their acceptable omissions, select methods and
environments, require independent checks, integrate cross-layer results, and
decide what the combined work can support.

These judgments are technical rather than ceremonial. An architecture is not
the union of locally successful component outputs. It is a choice of mechanisms
and interfaces that work together under conditions the product will encounter.
Architects must therefore inspect disagreement, exceptions, and model limits,
then determine which uncertainties the next design transition can carry.

The premise also changes how architects maintain technical contact with the
work. They need not perform every routine task manually, but they must remain
able to challenge a formulation, inspect decisive artifacts and failures,
trace a result across interfaces, and recognize when a model or check is being
used outside its support. Otherwise delegation removes the competence needed
to judge the design it produces.

## Architecture Result, Program Assessment, and Commitment

The two independent tests introduced in @sec-moonshot remain intact, and
commitment is a separate third decision. Architecture evidence establishes
what the design result supports under the required workload, software,
implementation, physical, and verification checks. A matched complete-workflow
comparison estimates the effect of adopting the full AI-assisted workflow
package against the strongest practical alternative. That package-adoption
estimate operationalizes the named AI-contribution test at the
complete-workflow level. It does not automatically isolate a causal
contribution from AI or any component. Isolation requires a controlled
replacement or ablation, and interactions among methods, tools, procedures,
and human work may leave the narrower contribution unresolved. Repeated
package-adoption results may then determine a broader program status. The
commitment authority separately decides whether the design, evidence limits,
organizational capacity, and residual risk justify commitment.

These judgments use related records but answer different questions. A
favorable architecture result does not demonstrate an AI contribution, and a
supported AI program does not authorize a design transition. Refusing a design
also does not by itself make the program unsupported. No result supplies
missing evidence for another judgment.

The program statuses developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect leave
different architecture actions open, so none determines the commitment by
itself (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program assessment** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
| --- | --- |
| Supported | The matched comparison showed that adopting the complete AI-assisted workflow package met the declared architecture-quality or total-cost improvement criterion. The architecture may still be refused because the design, evidence, capacity, or residual risk is unacceptable. |
| Unsupported | The matched comparison did not show the required package-adoption advantage. A sound architecture may still be committed on evidence produced by a conventional or human-directed workflow. |
| Unresolved | No workflow-package adoption claim is justified. The architecture may proceed only if independent design evidence supports it, or it may remain uncommitted while missing work is completed. |

: **Program assessment and architecture commitment remain independent.**
A favorable result on one cannot substitute for a favorable result on the
other. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

A supported program can still produce a design that should be refused, while
an unsupported program can leave a sound design backed by conventional work.
The table addresses only program status and commitment. It does not collapse
the architecture result into either. The rest of the chapter concerns the
evidence package, authority, and continuing responsibility needed for the
commitment decision.

## Framing the Architecture Problem

Architects do not enter only after a search finishes. Architecture begins
before the candidate set exists and continues after a local result looks
clean. The technical contribution lies in deciding what the system is, which
relationships matter, and which consequences the study must expose. Architects
also create or revise the mechanisms, interfaces, abstractions, and fallback
choices that make specialist results one coherent system. AI may participate
in that work, but the architecture question remains whether those pieces form
a feasible system that meets the product obligation.

Architects also help compose the AI-assisted workflow around that decision.
They determine which method may propose a change, which tool can measure the
relevant property, which check can stop a candidate, and which role resolves
disagreement among returned results. Those choices shape what the study can
observe and which conclusions it can support.

The Lighthouse prompt illustrates the first distinction. A prompt can state an
ambition, but an ambition is not yet an architecture problem. “Design a
low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR
workload” leaves open the representative workloads, supported software path,
product boundary, alternative designs, operating conditions, acceptable
tradeoffs, and decision to be made. Adding more words to the prompt does not
necessarily resolve those choices. Framing turns the ambition into a
challengeable technical question.

The framed problem also determines what the AI-assisted design system must
contain. A study about array utilization may need a cycle-level model and a
mapping search. A decision about freezing the array and its software-facing
interface must also expose compiler and runtime behavior, memory traffic,
implementation feasibility, subsystem power, and the consequences of later
change. The question determines the necessary abstractions and instruments,
not the other way around.

The judgments in @tbl-architect-technical-judgments describe the chapter's
technical spine. They can be informed by models, tools, and specialists, and
they may be distributed by subsystem, property, or design transition. A named
integration role must still determine whether the domain claims describe one
coherent product.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem choice and reframing | Is the stated problem still the one the product needs solved? | The task is not merely to maximize array utilization. It is to decide whether an implementation-facing compute and software interface meets the mobile XR obligation. |
| Abstraction | Which details can be simplified for this decision, and which must remain visible? | A cycle-level array model can compare mappings locally, but it cannot hide compiler behavior, memory traffic, physical timing, or the 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| System boundary | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet? | Array dimensions and dataflow cannot be separated from the runtime, interconnect, memory, energy, and implementation path they require. |
| Architecture synthesis | Do the mechanisms, interfaces, software path, implementation choices, and containment provisions form one feasible system? | The array, compiler and runtime interface, memory path, 3\ W constraint, and fallback behavior must form one implementable subsystem rather than separate local wins. |
| Missing constraints | What has the formulation, representation, objective, or tool path left out? | Representative workloads, interface cost, subsystem power, implementation feasibility, reliability and security properties, and containment remain open obligations. |
| Cross-layer tradeoff | Which feasible point best serves the product when objectives conflict? | Performance, energy, programmability, reversibility, schedule, and review burden must be composed rather than delegated to separate optimizers. |
| Mechanism and consequence | Does the proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens if it is wrong? | The failed directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor software contract and create costly RTL and physical rework. |
| Commitment under uncertainty | Are the remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting with the available organizational capacity? | The missing implementation-facing tests block the current freeze. The absent matched comparison independently leaves the AI program test unresolved. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** The
architect chooses the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before
deciding whether to commit. {#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

Problem choice, abstraction, and system boundary establish what counts as one
feasible system. The middle rows expose missing constraints and compose
cross-layer tradeoffs that separate specialist results cannot settle. The final
rows ask whether the proposed mechanism and remaining uncertainty support
commitment. The Lighthouse consequences show that these are acts of
architecture creation and technical synthesis, not approval after the design
is complete.

## Choosing Abstractions, Components, and Constraints

An abstraction is a technical choice about which details must remain visible
for a decision and which can be simplified without changing it. The same
candidate may be represented as an instruction mix, a dataflow graph, a
cycle-level model, synthesizable RTL, a floorplan, or a thermal model. None is
the architecture by itself. Each exposes some relationships and suppresses
others, so the architect chooses the representation whose omissions are
acceptable for the action under review.

This choice determines which components can contribute to the decision. The
architect asks what state each predictor, generator, optimizer, conventional
method, or tool may change and which independent observation constrains that
change. Adding components does not necessarily improve the composed system. A
component whose omissions hide a blocking property can make a result less
trustworthy even when its local output improves.

The public debate around the reinforcement-learning macro-placement method
later named AlphaChip supplies a concise component-versus-system example
[@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. A placement
method can produce strong candidate floorplans quickly. That capability does
not select the product floorplan on its own. The larger architecture and
implementation system still determines the block boundaries, macro set,
timing and power constraints, comparison basis, routability and signoff
checks, and whether the resulting placement serves the chip. A capable
component performs real design work while remaining one component of a larger
technical decision.

Architects also choose how these components interact. They decide which state
crosses an interface, which component may revise it, which independent result
can block progress, and whether two apparent checks share the same assumptions.
The arrangement changes which candidates can be proposed, which properties can
be observed, and which errors can survive.

Some consequential constraints first appear as expert judgment rather than
represented design state. This is *tacit knowledge*, the practical knowledge
that people use but cannot always state completely
[@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. A compiler specialist may know that a proposed
instruction has no efficient lowering in the supported toolchain. A physical
designer may recognize that a placement heuristic is unsafe for a particular
power-grid geometry and current profile.

AI can help locate, compare, and organize these judgments. It cannot make them
authoritative merely by writing them down. A consequential constraint,
assumption, or claim needs a check appropriate to its risk and scope. A
qualified automated method, conventional tool, specialist, or independent
reviewer may perform that check. A named accountable role still decides whether
the resulting constraint, assumption, or claim enters project state and owns
its scope, conflicts, expiration, and reopening.

@fig-tacit-extraction-bridge shows one specific path for tacit knowledge that
begins in situated human expertise.

![**Reviewing tacit domain knowledge before using it.** This path applies when a constraint begins as situated human expertise. A model can help elicit and organize it, but a named domain specialist challenges the proposed entry against records and tools. In this illustrated path, that specialist also holds the accountable role that decides whether the proposed constraint enters project state and owns its scope, conflicts, expiration, and reopening. Other technical claims may be checked by a qualified automated method, conventional tool, specialist, or independent reviewer as their risk and scope require.](images/F11b-tacit-extraction-bridge){#fig-tacit-extraction-bridge width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram showing domain knowledge passing through AI-assisted elicitation and domain validation before entering represented study state, with conflict, expiration, and new evidence returning the record for revalidation."}

In @fig-tacit-extraction-bridge, AI-assisted elicitation organizes documents,
assumptions, and contradictions. The named domain specialist challenges the
proposed constraint against records and tools because its basis is situated
expertise. The accountable role then decides whether it enters project state.
Its source, scope, affected interfaces, conflicts, and conditions for
reconsideration remain attached. New evidence prompts another technical review
rather than a silent overwrite.

Consider a physical designer's rule against placing two high-current macros on
the same power stripe. The geometry and current basis could become model state,
the threshold an environment constraint, and the violation a rejection check.
The decision about which macros justify the routing cost may still require
specialist judgment. A change to the power-grid template must prompt another
review rather than leave the rule in force as timeless expertise.

Not every expert intuition should become a formal rule. An unrecorded
constraint can be optimized away, while an overgeneralized one can reject good
designs. The distinctive architectural decision is whether the knowledge
belongs in model state, an environment constraint, a rejection check, or
specialist judgment.

## Integrating Across Layers and Disciplines

A candidate becomes an architecture only when its mechanisms and interfaces
work together across the layers that determine product behavior. For the
Lighthouse, this means connecting the XR workload and algorithms to the
compiler and runtime, instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture,
memory hierarchy and interconnect, RTL, physical design, package, power and
thermal limits, verification, and the user-facing product obligation. A local
improvement may have research or local value even when another layer cannot use
or implement it, but it does not yet establish a usable system result.

Search can find useful candidates and approximate a tradeoff frontier.
Choosing a point on that frontier is a different act. A wider network link may
improve camera-ingest latency while raising switching activity and routing
pressure. A narrower link may save dynamic power while increasing queueing or
software scheduling sensitivity. Some designs may improve both objectives
before the true tradeoff appears. The architect does not assume conflict in
advance. The architect determines which objectives, constraints, operating
conditions, and product consequences make one feasible point preferable to
another.

Finding the frontier is a search problem. Choosing a point becomes a product
commitment when it authorizes a consequential design transition. That choice
includes effects that no one optimizer may represent, such as software
turnover, difficult-to-reverse interfaces, verification capacity, package
constraints, field containment, or a user-experience threshold. A weighted
objective can encode a declared tradeoff, but it cannot decide whether the
weights still represent the product.

The architecture role composes specialist judgments rather than replacing
them. Compiler, verification, physical-design, and product specialists each
establish results within their own scope. The architect determines whether
those results address one coherent system decision and whether an interface
between them remains unexamined.

The technical process must preserve that coherence as work moves among people,
models, and tools. Candidate identity, assumptions, interfaces, checks, and
stopping conditions cannot disappear between components. The study boundary in
@fig-architect-owned-boundary carries the technical spine from
@tbl-architect-technical-judgments into delegated work.

![**Delegated work still requires architectural integration.** Models, tools, checks, and specialists may perform substantial parts of a study. The architecture role preserves the question, candidate identity, assumptions, independent checks, exceptions, stopping conditions, and commitment across that delegated work.](images/F11a-architect-owned-boundary){#fig-architect-owned-boundary width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture study containing delegated assistance, an architectural claim for review, supporting checks and records, and cross-cutting architecture decisions."}

The upper region places AI systems, tools, and specialists across substantial
execution and decision preparation. Assistance may prepare an analysis or
recommendation, but it cannot authorize commitment. The center holds the design
question, applicable conditions, supporting and conflicting results, and known
limits. Its supporting instruments qualify the central claim, and that
qualification informs but does not authorize commitment. The lower band carries
the table's architecture judgments across the complete study.

Delegation changes who or what performs the work. Integration preserves one
architecture question across that work. The lower band does not imply that
architects manually perform every step. It identifies the cross-cutting choices
that keep locally valid results from becoming an incoherent system.

## Interpreting Results and Disagreement

The account of feedback and verification in
@sec-feedback-verification-trust established how the scope, uncertainty, and
independence of a check
limit what its result can support. The architect's additional task is to
resolve what happens when those qualified results do not agree. A result may
support a local ranking while its failed mechanism explanation blocks transfer
to a changed workload, software path, interface, or implementation. The
architect must then narrow the claim, request a discriminating test, or keep
the dependent transition blocked.

The decision cannot be settled by counting votes. The responsible domain roles
must first determine whether the checks encode the same contract and conditions.
If they do, a blocking failure remains a failure. If they do not, the
architecture problem or interface definition must be corrected and the
affected paths rerun. When domain owners cannot reconcile the scopes, the named
integration role keeps the transition blocked and escalates the unresolved
system contract rather than choosing the more convenient result.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared
blocking property while the software model treats the same execution as legal.
The proposing system may not weaken the property, remove the failing workload,
or recast the counterexample as a pass. The first technical question is whether
the property and software model encode the same product contract. If they do,
the candidate fails. If they do not, the architecture problem must be corrected
and both paths rerun. The disagreement exposes a system-interface error that
neither local score can settle.

Interpretation connects each result to a consequence. A timing pass at one
corner cannot dispose of an open power-delivery failure, and a proof of a
declared property cannot show that the property captured the product behavior.
The system architecture role integrates these scoped judgments. It does not
replace the domain roles that establish verification, timing, physical,
power-integrity, safety, security, or reliability signoff.

Only after the architecture problem, integrated system, and meaning of the
results are clear can a design commitment be made.

## Making and Limiting a Design Commitment

An architecture commitment is a technical system choice. It selects a design
and its interfaces for further implementation, product integration, or
release under stated conditions. Commitment may be reversible during early
exploration and extremely expensive to reverse after an ISA, software
interface, floorplan, package, or mask set hardens. The evidence burden should
rise with that consequence.

The commitment states what design advances, which alternatives were rejected,
which conditions the evidence covered, which uncertainty remains, and what
would invalidate the choice. It does not certify that the design is perfect.
It establishes that the selected system is preferable to the credible
alternatives for the stated product obligation and that the remaining
uncertainty is bounded well enough for the next transition.

Three technical decisions must remain separate. Running work does not establish
what a result supports, and establishing support does not commit the
architecture (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights).

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execute design work | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Work stays within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. Execution cannot silently change a requirement or acceptance condition. |
| Establish what a result supports | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | The responsible technical role determines the result's scope and applicability. A waiver or later judgment cannot relabel a failed or inconclusive check. |
| Commit the architecture | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition? | The architecture decision composes alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, containment, and residual risk without replacing domain signoff. |

: **Execution, support, and commitment are different technical decisions.**
Separating them prevents a successful tool run or favorable local result from
silently authorizing the architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

The recorded result of a check remains unchanged. Later results can be added,
and changed conditions can invalidate whether the earlier result still applies
to the current candidate. The architecture role integrates these qualified
results but does not personally replace static-timing, physical-design,
verification, safety, security, or reliability signoff.

The assignment of these decisions differs across organizations. Their
technical meanings should not be collapsed. An AI-assisted system may perform
reversible actions and trigger declared stops, while the responsible technical
roles establish what its results support and the commitment authority decides
whether the system advances.

Those roles need enough expertise, access, and time to challenge the work they
accept. Otherwise review can become a blame-absorbing role
[@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones], and reviewers can exhibit automation bias
[@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. Direct access to decisive artifacts, an
independent first view, and periodic tests with known faults reveal whether the
challenge path remains credible. Automated proposal throughput is not
architecture throughput when qualified review cannot keep pace.

### Residual Risk and Containment

Commitment does not mean that every uncertainty disappeared. It means the
remaining failure modes are understood well enough to accept, mitigate, or
block. A bounded exception does not change the underlying result, and a
mandatory requirement remains blocking unless the requirement itself changes.
Residual risk is a technical property of the decision, not a label added after
the design advances.

A usable residual-risk statement identifies the failure mode, consequence,
uncertainty, detecting check, and containment or rollback action. If no check,
operating restriction, or containment path can detect or limit the failure,
the design transition remains blocked.

Consider a hypothetical optional Lighthouse vector-turbo mode whose subsystem
power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. Retaining the
circuitry for later study does not justify enabling the mode. A defensible
exception would require a verified disabled state, an enable path restricted
to an authorized lab or privileged service mode, verified reset, fault, and
access-control behavior, proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate
the base design's functional, timing, power, or security requirements, a named
owner, and an expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. If the
disabled state, isolation, or restricted enable path cannot be validated, the
feature is removed or the design does not advance. The exception does not turn
missing evidence into a pass. At expiration, a new decision must authorize
enablement from new evidence, renew a narrower exception, keep the mode
permanently disabled, or remove it.

Repeated exceptions can make a known failure look like the baseline, the
normalization of deviance described by Vaughan
[@Vaughan1996Challenger]. Expiration and reopening keep a temporary decision
from becoming permanent merely because the system stops reporting it.

### Design Containment Before Commitment

Containment authority matters only when the design contains a credible
technical lever. Depending on the failure, that lever may be a verified
feature-disable path, safe firmware fallback, derating mode, redundant
resource, isolation boundary, rollback path, or refusal to expose the
capability. Some failures have no safe containment short of repair or
replacement. The absence of a credible lever is itself a reason to refuse a
difficult-to-reverse commitment.

Disable mechanisms are not universal insurance. The disabled state must be
verified, the failure must be isolated from required behavior, and the control
path must remain available under the fault being contained. Errata and later
steppings provide established channels for describing and repairing some
silicon defects, but not every erratum has a workaround and not every later
revision fixes it.[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]

[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]: An erratum records a design defect or error that may
cause released silicon to deviate from published specifications, and it may
include a workaround when one exists. Intel's specification update also shows
that a later stepping may fix some errata while others remain unfixed
[@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate]. The record of an erratum or revision therefore does
not by itself establish containment or repair.

### Capacity to Challenge and Reopen

The organization must be able to challenge the decision it makes. Naming an
owner does not create this capacity. The candidate, conditions, alternatives,
results, disagreement, and current status must remain inspectable, and the
responsible roles need access to the artifacts and tools that could expose a
mistake.

Capacity can erode when automation removes the practice that once developed
it, the irony of automation identified by Bainbridge
[@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. This is not an argument for keeping routine work
manual. It is a reason to keep qualified reviewers in contact with tool
behavior, failed candidates, and cross-layer diagnoses so that the challenge
path remains technically credible.

Retained competence is observable. A qualified role can inspect the evidence,
reproduce or commission the decisive check, explain its assumptions and failure
modes, and recognize stale or out-of-scope results. Direct practice on selected
cross-layer diagnoses, examination of failed candidates, seeded faults, and
reassessment after a tool or architecture change can test whether this capacity
still exists and transfers to unfamiliar work.

Opaque external dependencies do not make responsibility disappear. A vendor
model, licensed IP block, process design kit, or commercial tool may limit what
the integrating team can inspect. The commitment must identify the exact
version, interface assumptions, available independent checks, and failures that
remain hard to diagnose. If those observations cannot support the required
claim or a safe fallback, commitment is unsound. A vendor certificate
establishes provenance, not an independent technical check.

### The Pending Lighthouse Commitment

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
The current evidence is insufficient for the Lighthouse target. The array
study's technical recommendation remains `awaiting_author_confirmation`, and
the commitment authority has not committed the design.
:::

The final assessment must keep the two retained records separate. The
prospective Lighthouse cache study did not run, so it supports no cache
measurement, baseline comparison, candidate recommendation, or implementation
claim. The separate array study evaluates five unique shapes under a synthetic
three-layer XR-like GEMM slice. It does not evaluate the full XR workload and
interface, the 3\ W subsystem target, or the pinned physical implementation
process. The array record therefore supports only its local comparison over
those five shapes.

Evidence is still missing for representative workloads, compiler and runtime
behavior, mapping, interface and memory cost, subsystem energy and power, RTL
behavior, physical implementation, security, reliability, and validated
containment. The next study must exercise the
representative workload and software path, measure the complete system
boundary, and complete the declared RTL, verification, physical, timing,
power-delivery, thermal, security, and reliability checks while preserving
their conditions, failures, cost, and acceptance limits.

A later commitment review needs the required coverage, system-boundary
measurements, implementation checks, and containment plan. A changed product
condition could instead make the candidate or question obsolete. The AI
program assessment remains separate and requires a matched comparison of
complete workflow packages. Technical review determines what the evidence
supports, while the named authority decides whether to act on it.

## Responsibility Continues

The unresolved Lighthouse work creates continuing responsibilities. Any role
receiving that work must receive the current status, its technical basis, and
the conditions that could support a later decision. Transferring responsibility
therefore means transferring the technical basis, not just the report.

The receiving role needs the exact candidate or release identity, the question
and system boundary, the assumptions and alternatives, the decisive passed,
failed, inconclusive, and missing results, the remaining uncertainty, and any
validated containment path. It must also know which workload, software, tool,
process, interface, or observed-behavior change would make the earlier decision
inapplicable. Proprietary access may limit reproduction, but the transfer must
still identify what only a protected reviewer could inspect.

The architect or named successor owns initiating technical reconsideration
when one of those conditions changes. That role does not personally repeat
every check. It ensures that the affected specialists reconsider the decision
and that an earlier result is not reused merely because its report remains
available. The detailed question of what transfers and which dependent work
must be repeated belongs to the transfer analysis developed in
@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack.

Observed failures can also reopen a commitment. Failing silicon establishes
that a failure occurred under the observed conditions, but not its root cause.
The technical investigation must still distinguish workload, software,
hardware, package, manufacturing, environmental, and operational explanations.

The Pentium FDIV case discussed in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive
illustrates the point. The public record supports missing lookup-table entries
and inadequate test coverage, but it does not reconstruct every internal
handoff. Its role here is narrower. Field evidence invalidated the confidence
behind a released design and demanded renewed architecture work, containment,
and a decision about the affected products.

## Open Research Questions

The questions across this book are not a complete research agenda. They are
prompts for forming better questions about what AI-assisted architecture should
make possible and what architects must still be able to judge.

**Sustaining architectural judgment.** Architecture education must preserve
direct contact with workloads, software, RTL, tools, and physical effects while
teaching students to use capable assistance.

- **Which mix of AI-assisted and direct practice preserves cross-layer
diagnostic ability and transfers it to unfamiliar design tasks?** A useful
evaluation must test whether architects can localize seeded and novel faults,
trace failures across layers, and reject invalid model assumptions after the
workload, tool path, or architecture changes.

**Responsibility in composed systems.** A design system can contain many
specialized people, models, and tools while producing one cross-layer result.

- **How can an AI-assisted design system detect and resolve incompatible
candidate identities, interface contracts, or operating assumptions before
dependent design work proceeds?** Individually qualified compiler, RTL,
simulation, and verification results can describe different candidates or
contracts. A benchmark could inject these mismatches and test whether the
system detects them, identifies affected work, and blocks dependent transitions
until the shared contract is reconciled.

- **When does incomplete visibility into a supplier component make an
architecture commitment unsound?** Vendor models, licensed IP, process
information, and tools can prevent direct inspection. Architects need a
technical boundary between opacity that independent interface checks can
contain and opacity that hides a failure mode essential to the system claim.

**Defining progress.** The broad test is whether assistance changes what
architects can reliably build, not merely how much activity can be automated.

- **Does AI assistance expand the class of computer systems that architects can
reliably design?** Answering this requires more than showing that existing work
runs faster. It requires evidence that previously impractical complexity can be
handled without weakening correctness, implementation quality, reversibility,
or technical responsibility.

These questions do not close the agenda. They mark problems that students,
researchers, and practitioners can enter. The next questions should make clear
what technical result would count as progress and whether it leads to systems
and decisions worth trusting.

## Closing the Moonshot

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
AI can perform substantial formulation, exploration, implementation, and
analysis. Architects still choose the problem, abstraction, boundary,
cross-layer tradeoff, and consequence that determine whether the resulting
design should be committed. They also keep that commitment valid by preserving
its conditions, containing failures, and reopening it when the evidence changes.
You can delegate the traversal of the design space, but you cannot delegate the
responsibility for the silicon.
:::

The chapter closes with a limited result. The current evidence is insufficient
for the Lighthouse target, the technical recommendation remains
`awaiting_author_confirmation`, and the commitment authority has not committed
the design. The AI program assessment is also unresolved because the matched
comparison of complete workflow packages has not been run.

If a later matched assessment supports the workflow package, the commitment
authority must still decide whether the selected design and its residual risks
justify commitment. If the assessment finds no package-adoption advantage, the
same architecture may still advance through a conventional workflow. A
component or narrower AI contribution remains unresolved when controlled
replacement or ablation cannot separate it from interactions. No one may turn
the absence of a verdict into a success claim.

Architecture 2.0 does not mean that AI independently designs computer systems.
It means that architects engineer and use an AI-assisted design system while
remaining responsible for the architecture problem, the cross-layer synthesis,
the consequential choice, and the continued validity of that choice. AI
extends the technical work that can be attempted. Architects decide whether
the resulting mechanisms and interfaces form one system worth building, then
reopen that decision when workloads, software, tools, process conditions,
products, or observed behavior change. That continuing technical work turns
capable automation into architecture.
